title: Trekking in Ethiopia: Full Guide
excerpt: The complete guide to our Ethiopia trek: the Simien Mountains and Ras Bwahit, the Danakil Desert and Tigray. Route, difficulty, season, visa and cost.
seoTitle: Simien Mountains and Danakil Trek: Route, Season, Visa and Cost

content.value: On the sixth morning of the journey, before sunrise, the group leaves Chennek camp in the Simien Mountains, at 3,620 m, and climbs to the summit of Ras Bwahit, 4,430 m (14,534 ft), the highest point of the whole journey. The Simien Mountains and Danakil Desert trek is a 12-day journey through northern Ethiopia: four walking days on the plateaus and cliffs of the Simien, three days in the Danakil Desert, one of the lowest and hottest places in the world, and a visit to the rock-hewn churches of Tigray. Previous trekking experience is not a requirement, but you need the fitness to walk 10 to 15 km a day at more than 3,000 m. The season runs from November to February.

In less than a week this journey takes you from grassy plateaus above 3,000 m, where troops of gelada monkeys graze at the edge of the cliffs, to salt flats below sea level and the colored sulfur fields of Dallol. This guide sets out what you need to know before deciding: what the Simien and the Danakil are, our route day by day, altitude and acclimatization, difficulty, season, visa and vaccinations, and what the price includes. And a word on a name many people search for: Ras Dashen, the highest mountain in Ethiopia, also stands in the Simien Mountains, but our trek does not climb it. The high point of our route is Ras Bwahit.

content.value: What the Simien and the Danakil are

The Simien Mountains are a high plateau in northern Ethiopia whose edges break away in walls of cliffs to the valleys below. Our trek runs within Simien Mountains National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, in the Amhara region. You walk along the edge of the cliffs, through fields of tall grass and giant lobelia plants, and the viewpoints open onto deep valleys and lone pinnacles rising out of them.

The Danakil Desert lies in the northeast of the country, in the Afar region, and it is a different world altogether: a desert depression, parts of which lie below sea level, with salt flats, volcanoes and fields of sulfur and minerals. On our route it comes after the mountains, so within a few days you go from the cold nights of the Simien to the heat of the desert.

The third part of the journey is the Tigray region in the north of the country, with ancient churches carved into the rock cliffs. You reach them from the city of Mekele and the village of Hawzen, at the end of the journey.
Our route, day by day
This is how the HighAir Simien Mountains and Danakil Desert trek is built. The altitudes in brackets are those of the overnight stop or of the high point of that day:

items: Day 1: arrival in Addis Ababa, a celebratory opening dinner and a briefing with the team.
Day 2: domestic flight to Gondar and a tour of the city: the 17th-century Royal Enclosure and the Debre Berhan Selassie church with its wall paintings.
Day 3: a drive to Debark (2,850 m), where the park permits are arranged, and the start of the trek to Sankaber camp (3,250 m).
Day 4: from Sankaber to Geech camp (3,600 m), by way of the Jinbar waterfall.
Day 5: the Imet Gogo viewpoint (3,900 m) and Inatye Peak (4,050 m), and a night at Chennek camp (3,620 m).
Day 6: the climb to the summit of Ras Bwahit (4,430 m), the descent and a drive to a hotel in Gondar.
Day 7: domestic flight from Gondar to Samara, changing planes in Addis Ababa, and a briefing for the desert days.
Day 8: a drive into the Danakil Desert, lunch facing Lake Afdera, and an evening walk up to the crater of the Erta Ale volcano. A night in tents at the foot of the mountain.
Day 9: the salt caravans and salt mining sites, the salt flats and Lake Asale, and a night in tents at Ahmed Ela camp.
Day 10: the Dallol depression, and a drive to Mekele, capital of the Tigray region.
Day 11: a drive to the village of Hawzen and a walk up to the rock-hewn churches, among them the church of Abraha we Atsbeha.
Day 12: domestic flight from Mekele to Addis Ababa, Merkato market and a traditional Ethiopian coffee ceremony, and the flight home.

content.value: On the four trekking days in the Simien you walk between 10 and 15 km a day, and walking time ranges from two or three hours on the first day to 7 to 9 hours on summit day. On the Danakil days most of the way is covered by jeep, 4 to 7 hours of driving a day, with short walks at the stops along the way.
Four days in the Simien Mountains

The trek starts in Debark, the gateway town to the park, where the entry permits are arranged. The park requires every group to go out with one of its scouts and a local guide. The first walking day is short: about 10 km and two to three hours of walking along the cliffs, with about 400 m of ascent to Sankaber camp, 3,250 m.

On the fourth day of the journey you walk 10 to 12 km to Geech camp, 3,600 m, on a trail of ups and downs along the edge of the cliffs. On the way you stop facing the Jinbar waterfall and look out over the open spaces of the park, and in the evening you watch the sunset over the mountains from the camp viewpoint.

On the fifth day you climb gradually to Imet Gogo, 3,900 m, one of the best known viewpoints in the park, and continue to Inatye Peak, 4,050 m. The ridge walk, 12 to 14 km, opens onto cliffs, green valleys and wide horizons, and at its end you reach Chennek camp, 3,620 m.

Summit day is the longest of the trek. You set out early in the morning, climb about 810 m to Ras Bwahit, 4,430 m, and walk about 15 km, 7 to 9 hours. From the summit, the highest point of the route, the views of the park open up, and after the descent to camp you leave the mountains and drive to Gondar, for a shower, a rest and a celebration of the end of the trek.
Geladas, Walia ibex and the Ethiopian wolf

Gelada monkeys are the emblem of the Simien. They live only in the highlands of Ethiopia, in large troops, and spend most of the daylight hours on the ground, in the grasslands at the edge of the cliffs. On our route you meet them on the very first walking day, and again on the way to Geech.

Other animals are rarer. The Walia ibex lives nowhere in the world but the Simien Mountains, and on the high ridges, on the way to Inatye and Ras Bwahit, we may see it. The same goes for the Ethiopian wolf, one of the rarest predators in Africa, and for the raptors soaring above the cliffs. No sighting of any of them is promised.

content.value: Three days in the Danakil Desert

After a night in Gondar you fly to Samara, changing planes in Addis Ababa, and the next morning you set out by jeep into the desert. On the way you stop for lunch facing Lake Afdera, and continue to the Erta Ale volcano. In the evening you walk up to the crater, a walk of up to an hour, with local guides and a security escort, as the local authorities require. The volcano's activity changes, and what can be seen in the crater, the lava lake included, depends on its state at the time of the visit. The night is spent in tents at a field camp at the foot of the mountain.

At dawn you drive to the village of Ahmed Ela. On the way camel caravans pass by carrying blocks of salt, and at the mining sites you see up close how the salt is broken, cut and loaded onto the camels. From there you continue to the salt flats and Lake Asale, one of the lowest places in the world, for sunset over the white salt crust.

On the third morning in the desert you reach the Dallol depression, a volcanic area where the colors of sulfur, minerals and acidic water rise from the ground in shades of yellow, green and brown. The water in the pools is acidic, so you walk only where the guides show you. From there you drive to Mekele, capital of the Tigray region.

content.value: The rock-hewn churches of Tigray

On the eleventh day you drive from Mekele, about an hour and a half, to the village of Hawzen in the heart of Tigray, and walk up to ancient churches carved into the rock cliffs. You visit the church of Abraha we Atsbeha and other sites in the area, and meet local priests in their traditional robes. On the last day you return to Mekele and fly to Addis Ababa, and before the flight home you visit Merkato market and take part in a traditional Ethiopian coffee ceremony, the buna.
Altitude and acclimatization

Even those who come to Ethiopia for the desert start the journey at altitude. Addis Ababa and Gondar both sit above 2,000 m, and on the trekking days in the Simien you sleep between 3,250 and 3,620 m and climb as high as 4,430 m. At these altitudes every breath brings in less oxygen, and the body needs time to adapt.

Altitude sickness usually starts with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue and nausea. On the high section of the Simien mild altitude symptoms are possible, which is why our itinerary is built for a gradual ascent: a night in Gondar, followed by three nights at camps that rise step by step, from 3,250 to 3,600 and 3,620 m. You meet Ras Bwahit, the high point, only on the last trekking day, and afterward you descend to sleep in Gondar, much lower down.

The rule in the mountains is simple: when symptoms get worse despite rest, you descend. In the mountains there is no promise of reaching every point, but there is always a commitment to safety above all. The group carries satellite equipment, travels with experienced local guides and keeps track of the weather, and the route may change according to the weather or the judgment of the guides on the ground.

content.title: ✦ From 4,430 m to below sea level
content.value: Within a few days you go from the summit of Ras Bwahit, 4,430 m, to the salt flats of the Danakil, which lie below sea level. The mountains call for warm clothing for the cold nights, and the desert calls for sun protection and plenty to drink.
How hard is the trek
We grade the trek as moderate. Its difficulty is a combination of four consecutive walking days at altitude, a long summit day, and after them the heat of the desert and the long jeep drives.

Previous trekking experience is not a requirement. If you can walk 10 to 15 km a day, enjoy a challenge and come with strong motivation, the trek can suit you. The best preparation is long hikes over rough ground, with climbs and a daypack, in the months before departure. A medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join.

In the Danakil the difficulty is different: not distance, but heat. In the months of our season the temperature in the desert reaches 35 to 40°C (95 to 104°F), and the challenge is to drink a lot, cover up from the sun and keep a calm pace. Mineral water is included throughout the journey.
Before departure you receive a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call.

Good to know: the journey is led by professional local guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the ground, is worth having. Every traveler must follow the instructions of the crew and take responsibility for their own safety throughout the journey.
When to go

Our departures to Ethiopia are between November and February. These are the months of the dry season in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, after the rainy season, which runs roughly from June to September. The trails are dry, and the weather in the Danakil is relatively bearable: 35 to 40°C, compared with close to 50°C in summer.

In the mountains the picture is reversed. At night in the camps above 3,000 m the temperature can drop to around zero and even below it, so warm clothing for the nights is part of the gear, even on a journey that ends in the desert. You will find the current departure dates on the trip page.
Before you set off

Northern Ethiopia has seen unrest in recent years, and several governments advise against travel to parts of the Amhara, Afar and Tigray regions. Check your government's current travel advice before booking and again before you fly, and make sure your travel insurance covers every area on the route.
Domestic flights and drives in the north of the country depend on the weather and conditions on the ground, so the route may change at the discretion of the local team.
Visa, vaccinations and permits

Most visitors, including UK, EU, US, Canadian and Australian citizens, need a visa for Ethiopia. The tourist e-visa is applied for on the official website of the Ethiopian government before the flight, and it costs 62 US dollars for a single entry of up to 30 days (as of 2026). The visa is not included in the price of the journey. Apply early, and make sure the details in the application match those in your passport.

Visit a travel clinic at least six weeks before the flight. Bring a yellow fever vaccination certificate: Ethiopia requires it from travelers arriving from, or transiting for a long time through, a country with a risk of the disease, and we ask every participant to carry one. Protection against malaria, and vaccination against typhoid, hepatitis A and polio, are also recommended, and the clinic will match the protection to the route. Vaccinations and travel clinic advice are not included in the price.
Entry permits for Simien Mountains National Park and for the other sites on the route are included in the price. The park permits are arranged in Debark, on the first trekking day.
What it costs and what is included

The Simien Mountains and Danakil Desert trek costs 3,000 US dollars per person. It includes airport transfers to the hotel in Addis Ababa and back, internal transfers to the start of the route and back, 4x4 jeeps with an open roof for up to 4 people each, domestic flights during the journey, 6 nights in 4-star hotels on full board, double tents with mattresses during the trek, three full meals a day throughout the trek, mineral water throughout the trek, professional local English-speaking guides, luggage transfers between overnight stops throughout the trek, showers and toilets during the stays in the field, all entry permits for the trek, a first aid kit with emergency oxygen cylinders, live WhatsApp updates for families during the trek, a personal area in the HighAir app, a detailed gear list and a training plan for the trek, an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide before departure, support with flight and travel insurance questions before departure, a gift kit with a cap and a dry-fit shirt, and a meaningful donation to the fight against cancer.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance with evacuation cover (required), personal gear (clothing and footwear), tips for the guides (50 dollars per person), the Ethiopia visa (62 dollars), an extra hotel night if needed, vaccinations and travel clinic advice, and personal expenses such as drinks, alcohol, laundry, gifts and internet. At extra cost you can add a single room at the hotels (50 dollars for the whole trek) or a solo tent during the trek (100 dollars for the whole trek).

Note that in the event of leaving the trip early, for any reason, the additional costs, such as extra hotel nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the traveler. Before buying insurance, check that the policy covers every area on the route and the altitude it reaches.

content.value: Who it suits

The Ethiopia journey suits those looking for more than a single trek: several days of walking in the mountains, days in a desert like no other, and an encounter with an ancient culture and history. It suits fit travelers who enjoy a challenge and are also ready for long jeep drives and very hot days in the desert. It suits less well those looking for a continuous walking journey from start to finish: four of the 12 days are full walking days in the mountains, and on the other days most of the time goes on drives, domestic flights and visits.

In terms of altitude, this is a trek at moderate heights, with a high point of 4,430 m. Anyone who discovers in Ethiopia that the mountains are for them can later think about a higher summit in Africa, Kilimanjaro, 5,895 m, about which we have written a complete guide.
Ethiopia with HighAir

At HighAir the Simien Mountains and Danakil Desert trek lasts 12 days, departs between November and February, and is limited to a group of up to 15 participants. Four days in the Simien with Ras Bwahit, three days in the Danakil with Erta Ale and Dallol, and the rock-hewn churches of Tigray. The success rate we publish for this journey is 92 percent.

A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Every climber who stands on the summits of the world started once, on one mountain. If the Simien Mountains are your mountain, we are here.
Frequently asked questions
How many days does the Ethiopia trek take?

The HighAir journey lasts 12 days, from arrival in Addis Ababa to the flight home. Four of them are walking days in the Simien Mountains, three are in the Danakil Desert, and the remaining days cover Gondar, the rock-hewn churches of Tigray and Addis Ababa.
How hard is the trek in the Simien Mountains?

We grade the trek as moderate. Walking days cover 10 to 15 km at more than 3,000 m, and summit day to Ras Bwahit, 4,430 m, takes 7 to 9 hours. Previous trekking experience is not a requirement, but good fitness, a medical certificate and a health declaration are.
How hot is the Danakil Desert?

In our season, November to February, the Danakil reaches 35 to 40°C, compared with close to 50°C in summer. Most of the time in the desert is spent in air-conditioned jeeps, and mineral water is included throughout the journey. Drink a lot, cover up from the sun and keep a calm pace.
Does the trek climb Ras Dashen?

No. Ras Dashen, the highest mountain in Ethiopia, stands in the Simien Mountains, but our trek does not climb it. The high point of our route is the summit of Ras Bwahit, 4,430 m, which you climb on the last trekking day.
What language do the guides speak?
The journey is led by professional local guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains.
